title: Machine Learning Basics
tagline: Teaching machines to learn from data rather than programming every rule by hand.

sections.content:
Machine learning (ML) is a subfield of artificial intelligence where systems **learn patterns from data** rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Instead of writing `if temperature > 30 then classify as hot`, you show the system thousands of labelled examples and it discovers the threshold itself.

There are three main paradigms. **Supervised learning** trains on labelled input-output pairs (e.g., images tagged cat/dog) and learns a mapping function. **Unsupervised learning** finds hidden structure in unlabelled data — clustering customers by purchasing behaviour, for instance. **Reinforcement learning** trains an agent by rewarding desirable actions and penalising bad ones, like training a game-playing bot through trial and error.

Understanding these paradigms, plus the vocabulary of **features**, **labels**, **training/test splits**, **overfitting**, and **gradient descent**, gives you the conceptual foundation to reason about any ML system.

sections.title: Teaching a Child to Recognise Cats
sections.content:
Supervised learning is like teaching a child to identify cats. You show them hundreds of pictures, saying 'cat' or 'not cat' each time. The child adjusts their internal mental model — updating what features (pointy ears, whiskers, fur patterns) matter. After enough examples they can correctly classify a cat they have never seen before.

Unsupervised learning skips the labels: you hand the child a pile of mixed animal photos with no guidance. They spontaneously group them by similarity — the fluffy ones here, the scaly ones there — without being told the category names.

Reinforcement learning is like training a dog with treats. The dog tries actions; correct actions get a treat (positive reward), wrong actions get nothing. Over many repetitions the dog learns the optimal strategy — without anyone ever explaining the rules.

**Features and labels** are the vocabulary of supervised learning. A **feature** is a measurable input variable: house square footage, age, pixel intensity, word frequency. A **label** is the output you want to predict: house price, disease/no-disease, spam/not-spam. The model learns a function `f(features) → label` from training examples.

**Train/test split** is critical for honest evaluation. You never evaluate a model on data it trained on — that is like grading students on the exact exam questions used during study. Typically 70-80% of data trains the model; the remaining 20-30% is held out as a test set to measure real-world performance. A **validation set** is sometimes carved out from training data to tune hyperparameters without touching the test set.

**Overfitting** occurs when a model memorises the training set rather than learning general patterns. A decision tree grown to full depth might perfectly classify every training example yet perform poorly on new data — it learned noise, not signal. Signs: training accuracy near 100%, test accuracy much lower. Fixes include regularisation, reducing model complexity, dropout (for neural nets), or gathering more training data.

**Underfitting** is the opposite: the model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data. A linear model fit to obviously non-linear data will have high error on both training and test sets.

**Gradient descent** is the workhorse optimisation algorithm. The model has parameters (weights) and a **loss function** that measures how wrong its predictions are. Gradient descent computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter — the direction of steepest increase — then steps in the *opposite* direction to reduce the loss. Repeat millions of times and the parameters converge to values that minimise prediction error.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The gradient descent loop computes mean squared error (MSE) loss and its partial derivatives with respect to w and b analytically. Each epoch updates both parameters by stepping opposite to their gradients. After 1000 epochs the parameters converge close to the true relationship (≈2x). The trainTestSplit utility shuffles randomly before splitting — shuffling prevents accidentally putting all high-value examples in one split.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Never evaluate on training data.** The single most common beginner mistake is reporting training accuracy as model performance. Always hold out a test set before you start, and touch it only once — at the very end. If you tune hyperparameters using the test set you inadvertently overfit to it. Use a separate **validation set** (or k-fold cross-validation) for tuning, and reserve the test set for a single final unbiased evaluation.

items: **Supervised learning** trains on labelled (features, label) pairs to learn a mapping function; **unsupervised learning** finds structure in unlabelled data; **reinforcement learning** learns by maximising cumulative reward through trial and error.
**Features** are input variables; **labels** are target outputs. Feature engineering — choosing and transforming the right inputs — often matters more than the choice of algorithm.
**Train/test split** gives an unbiased estimate of real-world performance. Never evaluate on training data; hold out the test set and touch it only once.
**Overfitting** = low training error, high test error. The model memorised noise. Fix with more data, regularisation, dropout, early stopping, or a simpler model.
**Gradient descent** iteratively adjusts model parameters in the direction that reduces the loss function, converging toward parameters that minimise prediction error on training data.

quiz.question: Which ML paradigm uses labelled (input, output) pairs to train a model?
options: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Self-supervised learning
quiz.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples — each input has a corresponding correct output (label). The model learns to map inputs to outputs. Unsupervised learning uses no labels; reinforcement learning uses a reward signal, not pre-labelled pairs.

quiz.question: What does 'overfitting' mean in machine learning?
options: The model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data
The model performs well on training data but poorly on unseen test data
The model was trained for too many epochs and the weights overflow
The training dataset is larger than the test dataset
quiz.explanation: Overfitting means the model has memorised the training data — including its noise — rather than learning generalisable patterns. It achieves high training accuracy but low test accuracy. The opposite (too-simple model, high error everywhere) is underfitting.

quiz.question: Why do we hold out a test set before training begins?
options: To reduce training time by using less data
To provide an unbiased estimate of real-world performance on data the model has never seen
To allow the model to train on harder examples last
To comply with data storage regulations
quiz.explanation: If the model is evaluated on training data, it will appear to perform better than it actually does in production. A held-out test set — never touched during training or hyperparameter tuning — gives an honest estimate of generalisation performance.

quiz.question: In gradient descent, what does the learning rate control?
options: The number of training examples used per step
The size of each parameter update step
The number of hidden layers in the model
The ratio of training data to test data
quiz.explanation: The learning rate (lr) scales the gradient when updating parameters: W = W - lr * gradient. Too large: oscillates or diverges. Too small: converges extremely slowly. Choosing a good learning rate (or using adaptive optimisers like Adam) is a key hyperparameter decision.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of unsupervised learning?
options: Classifying emails as spam or not-spam using labelled examples
Training a robot arm to assemble parts using a reward signal
Grouping customers by purchasing behaviour without predefined categories
Predicting house prices from historical labelled sales data
quiz.explanation: Grouping customers without predefined labels is clustering — a classic unsupervised learning task. The algorithm finds structure in the data without being told what categories exist. Spam classification and price prediction are supervised; robot training is reinforcement learning.

quiz.question: What is a 'feature' in machine learning terminology?
options: A desirable property of a model like accuracy or speed
A measurable input variable used to make predictions
The final output prediction of the model
A software module that handles data loading
quiz.explanation: A feature is a measurable input variable: pixel intensity, word count, temperature, age, etc. Features are what the model uses to make predictions. The output it predicts is the label (in supervised learning). Good feature engineering is often the biggest lever for improving model performance.

quiz.question: Reinforcement learning differs from supervised learning because:
options: It uses larger datasets
It learns from a reward signal via trial and error rather than labelled input-output pairs
It only works on image data
It does not update model parameters
quiz.explanation: In reinforcement learning there are no labelled pairs. An agent takes actions in an environment and receives rewards or penalties. Over time it learns a policy that maximises cumulative reward. RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) uses this approach to fine-tune large language models.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a validation set (as distinct from the test set)?
options: To train the model faster by providing easier examples first
To tune hyperparameters during development without contaminating the final test evaluation
To replace the test set when data is scarce
To store the model weights between training runs
quiz.explanation: If you use the test set to choose hyperparameters (learning rate, model size, etc.), you overfit to the test set and lose its unbiased nature. A validation set is held out from training but used during development for tuning decisions. The test set is touched only once for the final honest evaluation.

quiz.question: Which remedy is most directly targeted at overfitting due to excessive model complexity?
options: Increasing the learning rate
Using a larger training dataset or adding regularisation
Removing examples from the test set
Increasing the number of training epochs
quiz.explanation: Overfitting is caused by the model having too much capacity relative to the data. More data gives the model less opportunity to memorise noise. Regularisation (L1/L2) penalises large weights, discouraging extreme fits. Increasing epochs worsens overfitting; removing test examples is invalid.

quiz.question: In the gradient descent update rule W = W - lr * (dLoss/dW), what does the negative sign achieve?
options: It converts maximisation into minimisation
It moves parameters in the direction that decreases the loss, i.e., opposite to the gradient
It normalises the gradient to unit length
It prevents the parameters from becoming negative
quiz.explanation: The gradient points in the direction of steepest *increase* of the loss. Subtracting the gradient (moving opposite to it) therefore decreases the loss. This is gradient *descent* — descending the loss surface. Without the negative sign you would perform gradient ascent, maximising the loss instead.
